title: Ram, Allah, and Many Names
hookLine: a guru gives Kabir one name, Ram, and Kabir sings it beside Allah
carry: truth is one; the wise call it many names
tomorrow: if God's not in the temple or the mosque, then where?

lines: A FOOT IN THE DARK: RAM!
cards: Before dawn in Benares, a young weaver lies down on the steps of the river ghat, in the dark. A great teacher, Ramananda, comes down to bathe, steps on him, and cries out: Ram!
The legend says Kabir took that one word as his guru's gift, and you met that story back in year three. One word, from a guru: Ram. Here's what Kabir did with it.
In his songs, Ram isn't only the prince of Ayodhya. And the name sits beside others: Hari, Allah, Karim. Same song, same breath.

teach.h: HARI EAST, ALLAH WEST. MY GURU, MY PIR.
teach.b: Here's one song, in paraphrase, from the English version Tagore made. Hari is in the east, Allah is in the west. Look in your heart, and there you'll find both Karim and Ram.
It ends: he is my guru, he is my pir. Guru is the Hindu word for a spiritual teacher; pir is the Sufi one. Hindus have an old line that explains why this sounds like home to Hindu ears.
The Rig Veda says, in paraphrase: truth is one; the wise call it by many names. Ekam sat. That's why Hindu prayer is full of names.
Families chant the thousand names of Vishnu, and repeating the Name, japa, is itself worship. For Kabir, Ram was that one truth, beyond any form, and the Name was the whole path.
Islam honors many names too: the most beautiful names of God, Karim the Generous and Rahim the Merciful among them, all names of the one God, with no image.
That's an honest difference: Hindu names often come with forms and stories.
A couplet credited to Kabir, in paraphrase: the Hindu says Ram is dear to me, the Turk, meaning the Muslim, says Rahman, the Merciful; the two fought and died, and neither knew the secret.
So Kabir didn't coin a third word that swallowed both.
He kept each name whole, in its own tongue.

how: Hindus chant many names of God, from japa on a mala to the thousand names of Vishnu, and often quote the Rig Veda's line that truth is one and the wise call it by many names; Kabir's songs, with Ram and Hari beside Allah and Karim, are sung in Hindu devotional settings.

o: Hindu gurus who taught only at Persian courts
holy people both Hindus and Muslims remember as their own
Muslim saints whose shrines Hindus may not enter

p: truth is one, called by many names
the Hindu and Sufi words for a teacher
Islamic names: the Generous, the Merciful

s: the Rig Veda says truth is one, and the wise call it by many names
ekam sat: a line Hindus often quote when the names differ.
Kabir coined a new name for God to replace Ram and Allah
he kept each name in its own language, side by side.
in Kabir's songs, Ram means only the prince of Ayodhya
for Kabir, Ram names the one truth beyond any form.

games.q: a school interfaith night wants one welcome sign. a classmate suggests inventing a brand-new name for God that fits everyone. what would follow Kabir's pattern?
o: let each tradition's own words stand side by side on the sign.
pick the most familiar name so most people feel included.
leave every name off the sign, to be safe.
games.why: Truth is one, the wise call it many names, says the Rig Veda; Kabir kept each name whole, in its own tongue, rather than coining a third word that swallowed both.

practice: Japa is one of the oldest Hindu practices: repeating a name of God. If you pray, choose the name you grew up with, Ram, Krishna, Shiva, Ma, and say it slowly, eleven times, on your fingers or a mala.
Let each one land before the next. If you don't pray, use a word that means peace to you. Then, for one breath, hold in mind someone who calls the holy by a different name, and wish them well.

wordCard.voice: Hindu-Muslim shared saints. Here, a poet who called God by names from both homes, side by side.

orig.note: Sanskrit: ekam sat, truth is one; from the Rig Veda line that the wise call it by many names (1.164.46).

carryVoice: Keep this: truth is one, and the wise call it by many names. Kabir kept each one whole. That's today.

sources.ref: Legend of Kabir and Ramananda on the ghat steps (Ramananda steps on Kabir in the dark and cries 'Ram'), as told in hagiographies

Songs of Kabir (tr. Rabindranath Tagore, 1915), the poem beginning 'If God be within the mosque' (Hari in the east, Allah in the west; Karim and Ram in the heart; he is my guru, he is my pir) (poem number to confirm)
Rig Veda 1.164.46 (truth is one; the wise call it by many names)
Vishnu Sahasranama, the thousand names of Vishnu (Mahabharata, Anushasana Parva), chanted in Hindu homes and temples
Qur'an 7:180 (to God belong the most beautiful names); al-Karim and ar-Rahim among the traditional names of God
